VESPER: Online Learning of Free Energies
with a Multi-Tempered Variational Objective

Jay L. Kaplan    Gustavo R. Pérez-Lemus    Mengjian Hua    Juan J. de Pablo & Eric Vanden-Eijnden Affiliation: Equal advising. Affiliation: Courant Institute School of Mathematics, Computing, and Data ScienceNew York University, New York, NY 10012, USA Affiliation: Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, Tandon School of EngineeringNew York University, Brooklyn, NY 11201, USA Affiliation: Department of Physics, New York University, New York, NY 10012, USA Affiliation: Machine Learning Lab, Capital Fund Management*Corresponding authors: jjd8110@nyu.edu, eve2@cims.nyu.edu
Abstract

Computing molecular free-energy landscapes over collective variables (CVs) is central to understanding molecular mechanisms across physics, chemistry, and biology, but poses a difficult learning problem without training data available a priori. The microscopic potential is known, yet samples of the marginal CV distribution must be generated by molecular dynamics (MD), whose trajectories can remain trapped in metastable states and rarely cross the free-energy barriers governing conformational changes or chemical reactions. We introduce VESPER, which couples the generation of these samples to neural-network-driven free-energy learning: MD supplies configurations for learning, while the evolving model biases the MD to accelerate exploration and generate further training data. VESPER minimizes a single variational objective that is convex in the free energy and can combine several tempering levels, each using a distinct temperature-boosting factor to flatten the effective free-energy landscape and promote barrier crossing. Every level has the same physical free energy as its minimizer, allowing data from all levels to train one shared model without reweighting. Learning is driven by the difference in mean parameter gradients between biased MD configurations and auxiliary walkers that explore the flattened model directly in CV space. Replica exchange between levels can further accelerate exploration. We prove conditional convergence of the coupled overdamped population dynamics without replica exchange under log-Sobolev and Polyak–Łojasiewicz assumptions. VESPER matches or improves on established enhanced-sampling methods on alanine dipeptide and yields self-consistent free-energy reconstructions from three to six CVs on alanine tetrapeptide. For methane dehydrogenation on Ni(511) with a machine-learned interatomic potential, it recovers two-CV Boltzmann marginals and a reactant-to-saddle free-energy difference along a three-CV path, both qualitatively consistent with the lower-dimensional reference. It also samples RMSD-defined folded and unfolded regions of chignolin while biasing seventeen CVs.

1 Introduction

Molecular dynamics (MD) is a central tool for studying the structure and dynamics of molecular systems in physics, chemistry, and biology. A recurring goal is to compute the free-energy landscape over a set of informative collective variables (CVs), defined as the negative logarithm of their marginal density under the equilibrium distribution, multiplied by the thermal energy kB​Tk_{B}T. This landscape quantifies the relative stability of metastable states and the barriers separating them. Given samples from this marginal, learning it would be a standard estimation problem. In MD, however, the microscopic potential is known, but the relevant configurations must be generated by simulation. Brute-force MD is often computationally prohibitive: barrier-crossing transitions between metastable states can occur on microsecond-to-millisecond timescales, whereas integration requires femtosecond timesteps [Hénin et al., 2022]. Free-energy learning is therefore coupled to a sampling problem, and the model must accelerate the simulation while it is itself being learned.

We introduce VESPER (Variational Extended Space Parallel Ensemble Regression), which learns a neural free energy GθG_{\theta} while using it to bias the simulations that produce its own training data. VESPER minimizes a single variational objective: a positively weighted sum of components, one per tempering level, each using a distinct temperature-boosting factor to flatten the effective free-energy landscape. Each component is convex in the free energy and is minimized by the physical free energy at every such level. The sum therefore has the same minimizer up to an additive constant, and every level contributes its gradient to one model without reweighting to the physical ensemble. VESPER couples biased microscopic dynamics, persistent auxiliary CV walkers, and free-energy learning through one shared model. Through the CV map s⁡(x)s(x), the same GθG_{\theta} sets both the MD bias and the tempered auxiliary potential, with no separate free-energy recursion. We also establish conditional convergence of the coupled sampling and learning dynamics. These contributions build on established variational connections: individual components extend the pseudo-spherical family to negative exponents and admit Rényi variational forms [Yu et al., 2021, Fujisawa & Eguchi, 2008, Birrell et al., 2021], and their gradients recover the instantaneous update of well-tempered variationally enhanced sampling (VES), up to scale, when its target is held fixed during differentiation [Valsson & Parrinello, 2014, Valsson & Parrinello, 2015, Bonati et al., 2019].

The gradient of each component is the difference between two averages of ∇θGθ\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}: one over MD configurations evolving under the microscopic potential plus a bias built from GθG_{\theta}, the other over persistent auxiliary walkers evolving directly in CV space under a tempered GθG_{\theta}. At the optimum both populations sample the same flattened distribution, and the walkers interact with the molecular system only through the shared parameters, so no adiabatic limit is needed to identify the free energy, unlike in temperature-accelerated MD and driven adiabatic free-energy dynamics [Maragliano & Vanden-Eijnden, 2006, Abrams & Tuckerman, 2008]. Replica exchange can additionally carry configurations discovered under strongly flattened biases down the ladder, facilitating barrier crossing along the CVs.

Our main contributions are:

  • •

    A single objective with a common minimizer. We establish that the losses associated with all tempering levels are convex in the free-energy function and share the physical free energy as their minimizer, up to an additive constant. Their positively weighted sum therefore defines one objective for one model, with every level contributing its native gradient without reweighting to the physical ensemble (Proposition 1).

  • •

    Online learning from coupled sampling populations. Biased MD and persistent auxiliary CV walkers generate the configurations needed for learning as the model evolves, without a pre-existing dataset or an adiabatic limit between microscopic and auxiliary coordinates. We prove conditional convergence of the coupled overdamped population dynamics without replica exchange under log-Sobolev and Polyak–Łojasiewicz assumptions, controlling both objective error and sampling lag (Section A.6).

  • •

    Replica exchange on the learned free energy. The Metropolis acceptance probability for exchange between adjacent levels depends only on learned free-energy differences in lower-dimensional CV space, avoiding additional evaluations of the microscopic potential. At a fixed model, the exchange kernel preserves the product of the sampling laws across levels and therefore leaves the population gradient unchanged.

  • •

    Controlled tests of tempering and replica exchange. On the Müller–Brown potential, the tempering ladder balances basin accuracy, measured by KL divergence, with landscape reconstruction, measured by RMSE. On four-well landscapes spanning two to one hundred dimensions, a fixed ladder remains competitive without dimension-specific selection of α\alpha, with replica exchange improving accuracy and convergence in the most challenging high-dimensional case (Section 3.1).

  • •

    Molecular free-energy reconstruction and high-dimensional exploration. On alanine dipeptide, VESPER achieves competitive reconstruction accuracy and convergence relative to the tested enhanced-sampling baselines. On alanine tetrapeptide, agreement between Boltzmann marginals learned with three and six CVs demonstrates dimensional self-consistency. For methane dehydrogenation on Ni(511) with a machine-learned interatomic potential, VESPER learns a three-CV landscape whose two-CV Boltzmann marginals and reactant-to-saddle free-energy difference along a three-CV path are consistent with the lower-dimensional reference. On chignolin, biasing seventeen dihedral CVs produces repeated RMSD-defined unfolding and refolding transitions, demonstrating effective exploration of a high-dimensional molecular CV space (Section 3).

2 Methodology

2.1 Collective variables and free energy

Let x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} denote a molecular configuration, U⁡(x)U(x) its microscopic potential energy, and ϱ⁡(x)=Z−1​e−β​U​(x)\varrho(x)=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta U(x)} its equilibrium density at inverse temperature β=(kB​T)−1\beta=(k_{B}T)^{-1}. A collective-variable map s:𝒳→𝒮s:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{S} reduces the dd-dimensional configuration space to a DD-dimensional CV domain, typically with D≪dD\ll d. The equilibrium CV density and its associated free energy are

p⁡(s)=∫𝒳δ⁡(s−s⁡(x))​ϱ​(x)​𝑑x,G⋆​(s)=−β−1​log⁡p⁡(s).p(s)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\delta(s-s(x))\varrho(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad G_{\star}(s)=-\beta^{-1}\log p(s). (1)

The microscopic potential supplies the forces for simulation, whereas the marginal p⁡(s)p(s) must be inferred from configurations generated by the simulation. VESPER represents G⋆G_{\star} by a differentiable model GθG_{\theta} and uses it to bias the molecular dynamics that generate its training configurations.

2.3 The combined objective

Choose 0≤β^1<⋯<β^K≤β0\leq\hat{\beta}_{1}<\cdots<\hat{\beta}_{K}\leq\beta, set αk=β^k/β\alpha_{k}=\hat{\beta}_{k}/\beta, and write PG,kP_{G,k}, νG,k\nu_{G,k}, QG,kQ_{G,k} for the laws of level kk. At β^k=β\hat{\beta}_{k}=\beta and, on compact 𝒮\mathcal{S}, at β^k=0\hat{\beta}_{k}=0, define the endpoint objectives directly under the endpoint conditions in Section A.2:

ℒβ​[G]=1β​log​∫𝒮e−β​G​(s)​𝑑s+𝔼p​[G],ℒ0​[G]=−𝔼u​[G]+1β​log​𝔼p​[eβ​G].\mathcal{L}_{\beta}[G]=\frac{1}{\beta}\log\int_{\mathcal{S}}e^{-\beta G(s)}\,\mathrm{d}s+\mathbb{E}_{p}[G],\qquad\mathcal{L}_{0}[G]=-\mathbb{E}_{u}[G]+\frac{1}{\beta}\log\mathbb{E}_{p}\bigl[e^{\beta G}\bigr]. (8)

2.4 Coupled sampling and optimization

We estimate the expectations in equation 10 with two populations at each level, all sharing GθG_{\theta} (Fig. 1). At level kk, nkn_{k} physical walkers evolve under the biased potential U⁡(x)−(1−αk)​Gθ​(s⁡(x))U(x)-(1-\alpha_{k})G_{\theta}(s(x)), and NkN_{k} auxiliary walkers evolve directly in CV space under the tempered potential αk​Gθ​(s)\alpha_{k}G_{\theta}(s):

where ms,mxm_{s},m_{x} are masses, γs,γx\gamma_{s},\gamma_{x} friction coefficients, and ηti,k,η~tj,k\eta_{t}^{i,k},\tilde{\eta}_{t}^{j,k} independent white noises. The bias force on the molecular system is ∇xGθ​(s⁡(x))=Js​(x)⊤​∇sGθ​(s⁡(x))\nabla_{x}G_{\theta}(s(x))=J_{s}(x)^{\top}\nabla_{s}G_{\theta}(s(x)), with Js=∂s/∂x∈ℝD×dJ_{s}=\partial s/\partial x\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times d}. For fixed θ\theta, these dynamics have configurational invariant laws PGθ,kP_{G_{\theta},k} and νGθ,k\nu_{G_{\theta},k} (Section A.3), so their walker averages estimate the two expectations in equation 10. The parameters follow the corresponding gradient flow with γθ−1\gamma_{\theta}^{-1} the learning rate,

γθ​θ˙t=∑k=1Kck​[1Nk​∑i=1Nk∇θGθt​(sti,k)−1nk​∑j=1nk∇θGθt​(s⁡(xtj,k))].\gamma_{\theta}\dot{\theta}_{t}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}c_{k}\left[\frac{1}{N_{k}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{k}}\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta_{t}}(s_{t}^{i,k})-\frac{1}{n_{k}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{k}}\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta_{t}}(s(x_{t}^{j,k}))\right]. (12)

Three features of this construction matter in practice.

  • •

    Timescales. Since θ\theta moves, the walkers track moving targets, and the averages in equation 12 approximate the gradient when θ\theta evolves more slowly than the walkers relax. Section A.6 makes this quantitative for the overdamped dynamics: objective error and sampling lag decay together when the learning rate is below a threshold set by the log-Sobolev constants of the sampling laws and a bound on the parameter gradients, so no adiabatic limit is needed.

  • •

    Cost. Auxiliary walkers live in the DD-dimensional CV space and need one network evaluation per step, so NkN_{k} can be large (10410^{4}–10510^{5} in the molecular runs) with cost dominated by the biased MD.

  • •

    Persistence. Auxiliary walkers persist between parameter updates, as in persistent contrastive divergence [Tieleman, 2008], staying close to equilibrium in the slowly changing tempered model.

Section A.6 derives a conditional convergence bound for the coupled overdamped population dynamics without replica exchange. For 0<αk<10<\alpha_{k}<1, define Vt=F⁡(θt)−F∗+HtV_{t}=F(\theta_{t})-F_{*}+H_{t}, where F=β​ℒVESPERF=\beta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VESPER}} and HtH_{t} is the weighted KL sampling lag defined in equation 35. Under assumptions (C1)–(C4), for 0<η<a/B20<\eta<a/B^{2},

Vt≤e−κ​t​V0,κ=2​min⁡{η​μ,a−η​B2}.V_{t}\leq e^{-\kappa t}V_{0},\qquad\kappa=2\min\{\eta\mu,a-\eta B^{2}\}. (13)

Thus objective error and sampling lag decay together. Under (C1)–(C3), the same learning-rate restriction gives the time-averaged stationarity bound

1T​∫0T‖∇F​(θt)‖2​𝑑t≤V0η​T.\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\|\nabla F(\theta_{t})\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\leq\frac{V_{0}}{\eta T}. (14)

In the implementation, equation 12 is discretized: sampling epochs alternate with optimizer steps, and batches may be reused across several steps with within-batch importance weights (Algorithm 1, Section B.7). When equilibrium configurations from ϱ\varrho are available, the physical average can instead be computed from them with self-normalized weights (Section A.9).

2.5 Replica exchange across tempering levels

The common-minimizer property does not require the levels to communicate. Sampling, however, benefits from it: strongly flattened levels cross barriers readily, while weakly flattened ones, including the physical level, may remain trapped. We therefore couple adjacent levels by replica exchange [Sugita & Okamoto, 1999, Affentranger et al., 2006, Earl & Deem, 2005], performed between parameter updates with GθG_{\theta} held fixed. For a symmetric swap proposal between levels ii and jj, the Metropolis acceptance probability for physical walkers is

Ax​(xi,xj)=min⁡{1,exp⁡[(β^i−β^j)​(Gθ​(s⁡(xi))−Gθ​(s⁡(xj)))]},A_{x}(x^{i},x^{j})=\min\!\left\{1,\exp\!\left[(\hat{\beta}_{i}-\hat{\beta}_{j})\bigl(G_{\theta}(s(x^{i}))-G_{\theta}(s(x^{j}))\bigr)\right]\right\}, (15)

and As​(si,sj)A_{s}(s^{i},s^{j}) is identical with s⁡(xi)s(x^{i}), s⁡(xj)s(x^{j}) replaced by sis^{i}, sjs^{j}. Each swap preserves the fixed-model target product law ∏kνGθ,k\prod_{k}\nu_{G_{\theta},k} or ∏kPGθ,k\prod_{k}P_{G_{\theta},k}, and hence the population-gradient identity (Section A.5). All physical replicas share the same potential UU and thermostat temperature, so the microscopic energy and Maxwell factors cancel from the exchange ratio. Both acceptance ratios therefore depend only on the learned free-energy differences in CV space. Given the CV values, their evaluation requires only two model values and no additional microscopic-energy evaluation. The tempering-level spacing is controlled by fluctuations of GθG_{\theta}, which can depend on the system and choice of CVs. Physical and auxiliary swaps are proposed independently.

2.6 Related work

Adaptive-bias enhanced sampling.

Umbrella sampling, adaptive biasing force, metadynamics and its well-tempered variant, and on-the-fly probability enhanced sampling accelerate MD with restraining or adaptively built CV-dependent biases during the simulation [Torrie & Valleau, 1977, Darve & Pohorille, 2001, Darve et al., 2008, Laio & Parrinello, 2002, Barducci et al., 2008, Invernizzi & Parrinello, 2020]. Neural representations of the free energy or bias have been trained from mean forces, histograms, or both [Schneider et al., 2017, Sidky & Whitmer, 2018, Guo et al., 2018, Sevgen et al., 2020, Zubieta Rico et al., 2025]. Reinforced dynamics couples such training to an uncertainty-gated bias [Zhang et al., 2018]. VESPER couples biased MD and persistent auxiliary CV walkers through one physical free-energy model, with all tempering levels contributing to an objective with a common minimizer (Proposition 1). Its closest variational connection is to variationally enhanced sampling (VES) [Valsson & Parrinello, 2014], in its well-tempered [Valsson & Parrinello, 2015] and neural [Bonati et al., 2019] forms. With bias Vθ=−(1−α)​GθV_{\theta}=-(1-\alpha)G_{\theta} and target tθ∝e−α​β​Gθt_{\theta}\propto e^{-\alpha\beta G_{\theta}} held fixed during differentiation, the VES gradient equals (1−α)​∇θℒβ^​[Gθ](1-\alpha)\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G_{\theta}] (Section D.1). VESPER gives this instantaneous update an explicit objective in the physical free energy, with the current model directly determining both the molecular bias and the auxiliary target, without a separate recursive free-energy estimate. Neural VES also evaluates target averages by numerical integration or Monte Carlo. Here, persistent auxiliary dynamics form part of the coupled learning system (Section A.6).

Replica ladders with CV biases.

Replica exchange improves exploration by swapping configurations between replicas with different temperatures or Hamiltonians [Sugita & Okamoto, 1999, Affentranger et al., 2006, Earl & Deem, 2005]. Bias-exchange metadynamics assigns different CVs to different replicas [Piana & Laio, 2007]. Replica exchange with collective-variable tempering uses a ladder of well-tempered biases of increasing strength, which is the closest analogue of VESPER’s physical population [Gil-Ley & Bussi, 2015]. VESPER uses the ladder for joint free-energy learning as well as configuration exchange: every level supplies its native gradient to one shared model, and the common-minimizer property allows these contributions to be combined without reweighting between levels (Proposition 1).

Extended-variable methods.

Temperature-accelerated MD, driven adiabatic free-energy dynamics, and related schemes couple the CVs to hot auxiliary variables through a stiff spring. They recover the free energy in the limit of adiabatic separation between auxiliary and molecular motion [Maragliano & Vanden-Eijnden, 2006, Abrams & Tuckerman, 2008, Rosso et al., 2002, Chen et al., 2012, Awasthi & Nair, 2017], possibly followed by mean-force reconstruction [Maragliano & Vanden-Eijnden, 2008]. VESPER identifies the physical free energy through its variational minimizer, without requiring an adiabatic limit between auxiliary and molecular coordinates. Its auxiliary walkers explore the tempered model and communicate with the molecular system through shared parameters, without a spring coupling between the two populations.

Energy-based models and tempered objectives.

VESPER connects tempered energy-based learning to molecular simulation through the prescribed CV map s⁡(x)s(x). Biased microscopic dynamics generate the tilted CV law, while persistent auxiliary walkers sample the tempered model directly in CV space [Hinton, 2002, Tieleman, 2008]. Both populations train the same physical free-energy model without a pre-existing equilibrium dataset (Section A.3). With g=β​Gg=\beta G and γ=α−1\gamma=\alpha-1, the single-level objective takes the form of the pseudo-spherical contrastive divergence (PS-CD) objective [Yu et al., 2021], built on the γ\gamma-cross-entropy [Fujisawa & Eguchi, 2008], continued to negative γ\gamma, and admits a Rényi variational representation [Birrell et al., 2021]. At α=1\alpha=1 it reduces to maximum likelihood. For 0<α<10<\alpha<1, VESPER uses the negative branch γ=α−1∈(−1,0)\gamma=\alpha-1\in(-1,0). The factor qθγq_{\theta}^{\gamma} relatively upweights observations in regions of low model density and high model free energy. At the physical solution, both populations have CV densities proportional to pαp^{\alpha}, scaling CV free-energy barriers by α\alpha and increasing the relative weight of rare regions (Appendix D). PS-CD estimates its positive term from a fixed dataset and its tempered model term by importance weighting model samples [Yu et al., 2021]. VESPER realizes both tilted laws through coupled dynamics, extending this variational principle to simultaneous molecular sampling and free-energy reconstruction (Appendix D). Parallel tempering has also been used to train restricted Boltzmann machines [Desjardins et al., 2010, Cho et al., 2010], with only the untempered chain entering the gradient. In VESPER every level contributes.

Learned samplers.

Boltzmann generators and non-equilibrium transport samplers learn maps or flows that sample a known energy [Noé et al., 2019, Dibak et al., 2022, Invernizzi et al., 2022, Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2025], and annealed importance sampling and Jarzynski-type estimators weight paths between distributions [Neal, 2001, Jarzynski, 1997, Carbone et al., 2023]. These methods target the full configurational distribution. VESPER instead targets a CV free energy through directly simulated tilted populations.

3 Numerical results

We evaluate VESPER on analytic landscapes and molecular systems to test free-energy reconstruction accuracy, convergence as the number of CVs increases, and exploration of conformational and chemical changes in complex MD systems. The analytic benchmarks provide exact references and controlled comparisons of tempering and replica exchange, while the molecular applications test the method in realistic MD. Complete simulation settings and numerical comparisons are given in the appendices. Molecular simulation times are per replica. Aggregate MD and population budgets are specified in Tables 2 and C.2.

3.1 Analytic landscapes: tempering and increasing dimension

The Müller–Brown benchmark [Müller & Brown, 1979] tests how tempering balances accuracy in low-energy basins with reconstruction over a broader region of the landscape, including high-free-energy regions of low probability mass (Fig. 2A–C). Moderate tempering gives the lowest basin-sensitive KL divergence, while stronger tempering gives the lowest full-domain RMSE. The fixed exchange ladder balances these objectives, reaching a KL divergence of 0.017±0.0130.017\pm 0.013 while keeping its mean RMSE within 1%1\% of the lowest tested value. Here the RMSE includes extrapolation beyond the simulation box into a high-energy rim, so it measures broad-domain reconstruction rather than barrier accuracy alone (Section C.1).

We then increase the dimension of a rotated four-well landscape from two to one hundred, keeping the hidden width, walker budget and update schedule fixed (Fig. 2D–F). The same tempering ladder remains competitive across the tested dimensions without selecting a different tempering strength for each problem. At one hundred dimensions, the exchange ladder gives the lowest mean normalized RMSE among the primary comparisons: 0.32±0.210.32\pm 0.21, compared with 0.42±0.050.42\pm 0.05 for the best tested single level. These results support using a shared ladder across dimensions, with its strongest advantages appearing in the more demanding exploration problem. The landscape, averaging conventions and larger-population controls are specified in Section C.2.

3.2 Alanine dipeptide: comparison with established methods

Alanine dipeptide (ADP) in explicit water tests whether VESPER can reconstruct a molecular free-energy surface with accuracy and convergence comparable to established enhanced-sampling methods. With the two backbone dihedrals (ϕ,ψ)(\phi,\psi) as CVs, tempered VESPER explores the periodic landscape and recovers the reference surface [Zubieta Rico et al., 2025], while the unbiased control remains concentrated in its initial basin (Fig. 3). At 1010 ns per replica, the exchange ladder reaches an RMSE of 2.02±0.242.02\pm 0.24 kJ mol-1, comparable to 2.04±0.512.04\pm 0.51 kJ mol-1 for SIREN-based combined force-frequency sampling (S-CFF), the strongest tested baseline at that horizon. A single tempered level also performs well. The ladders make only a small change to the endpoint error on this relatively simple low-dimensional landscape.

The VESPER mean error curves first fall below 11 kcal mol-1 and remain there through 1010 ns at approximately 2.02.0 ns for a single level and 1.81.8–1.91.9 ns for the ladders. Metadynamics and S-CFF reach this threshold earlier, at 1.31.3–1.41.4 ns. VESPER therefore combines comparable late-time accuracy with rapid practical convergence, within about 22 ns, on this benchmark. Full baseline comparisons and scoring conventions are given in Sections B.1, B.9 and 3.

3.3 Alanine tetrapeptide: consistency as the number of CVs increases

Alanine tetrapeptide (ATP) tests whether VESPER retains a consistent molecular description when the number of biased backbone dihedrals increases from three to six. The two models differ only in their input layer, and their two-dimensional Boltzmann marginals retain similar broad structure (Fig. 4). Both six-CV ladder variants also produce more consistent learned shapes between 55 and 1010 ns than the selected single-level model: the correlations with their own 1010 ns estimates are 0.913±0.0120.913\pm 0.012 with exchange and 0.941±0.0280.941\pm 0.028 without, compared with 0.804±0.1790.804\pm 0.179 for the single level. This suggests that multiple learning levels can stabilize reconstruction over the observed interval in the higher-dimensional six-CV model. Without an independent converged six-CV reference, these comparisons establish dimensional and temporal consistency.

3.4 Catalytic methane dehydrogenation on Ni(511)

We next test VESPER on a reactive free-energy landscape described by a machine-learned interatomic potential. For methane on Ni(511) at 700700 K, a single tempered level learns a joint surface over the C–Ni and C–H coordination numbers and the carbon atom’s lateral position. Its two-CV Boltzmann marginals recover the physisorbed and dissociated basins and the transition region of the lower-dimensional reference [Jin et al., 2025] (Fig. 5).

The differentiable neural representation also supports post hoc analysis of the joint three-CV landscape using its gradients. A string-method path calculation [E et al., 2007], followed by constrained gradient-flow refinement, connects reactant and product through a fitted saddle. The bounded reactant-to-saddle free-energy difference is 1.12±0.251.12\pm 0.25 eV, consistent with the reference. Including the lateral position directly in the model locates the fitted saddle near the step-edge atoms. Whereas Jin et al. [2025] obtained an additional spatial free-energy description through post hoc Spectral-ABF analysis of existing trajectories, VESPER learns the joint three-CV surface during sampling. The route, averaging and projection conventions are specified in Section B.5.

3.5 Chignolin: exploration with seventeen CVs

Finally, we test whether one shared neural free energy can support exploration in the high-dimensional space of chignolin’s seventeen backbone dihedrals. For CLN025 in explicit water, a twelve-level ladder continuously trains the joint model during replica exchange, with every level contributing to learning (Fig. 6). The representation is not restricted to a sum of pairwise terms, and the target is not prescribed as a folded/unfolded mixture, extending earlier work on this system [Shaffer et al., 2016].

Starting from folded configurations, VESPER explores RMSD-defined folded and unfolded regions. Exploration broadens along the ladder while the unbiased level remains predominantly folded. Auxiliary-sample projections place the free-energy minimum in the folded region and represent a broader range of conformations also visited by MD. VESPER thus learns a joint free energy while exploring conformational changes with seventeen CVs.

4 Discussion and conclusion

We introduced VESPER, which casts free-energy learning and enhanced sampling as a single optimization problem. The free energy is parameterized by a neural network GθG_{\theta} that biases the MD, drives tempered auxiliary walkers in CV space, and is trained on the difference between its mean parameter gradients over the auxiliary walkers and the biased MD configurations. This difference estimates the gradient of one variational objective, so the simulation generates its own training data as the model improves. Working in an extended space of molecular configurations and auxiliary walkers, VESPER minimizes an explicit objective whose minimizer is the physical free energy itself. The free energy is therefore learned directly, rather than recovered from a bias optimized toward a fixed or recursively updated target, and no adiabatic separation between auxiliary and molecular coordinates is required. Because the objective is convex and every tempering level shares the same global minimizer, all levels train one model without reweighting between them. Strongly flattened levels that cross barriers readily therefore work alongside weakly tempered levels, and when the ladder includes the physical level, α=1\alpha=1, the ladder objective bounds the KL divergence of the model from the true CV distribution. Replica exchange moves configurations along the ladder using only learned free-energy differences in CV space, with no additional evaluations of the microscopic potential. The coupled sampling and learning dynamics also carry a conditional convergence guarantee.

VESPER is effective across a wide range of problems. The analytic landscapes provide exact references for controlled tests. On the Müller–Brown potential, the exchange ladder balances accuracy in the low-energy basins with reconstruction of the broader landscape. On a four-well landscape whose dimension grows from two to one hundred, one fixed ladder stays competitive without retuning and shows its clearest advantage at one hundred dimensions. Alanine dipeptide is a standard molecular benchmark with a reference surface for direct comparison. Here VESPER matches or improves on the accuracy of established enhanced-sampling methods, reaching the end-point error of the best tested baseline, and converges within 22 ns. Alanine tetrapeptide tests whether the learned description stays consistent as more CVs are biased, and the Boltzmann marginals learned with three and six CVs agree. Methane dehydrogenation on Ni(511) extends the tests from conformational to chemical change, using a machine-learned interatomic potential. VESPER learns a reactive three-CV landscape whose two-CV marginals recover the basins and transition region of the reference. Because the model is a differentiable neural network, a string-method calculation with gradient-flow refinement then maps the reaction path directly on the joint three-CV surface learned during sampling. Chignolin tests exploration in a realistic high-dimensional CV space. While biasing seventeen backbone dihedrals, one shared model drives repeated unfolding and refolding. These results connect online free-energy learning to enhanced sampling across conformational and chemical changes. Molecular comparisons retain their per-replica cost: a KK-level ladder uses KK times the aggregate MD of a single replica at the same horizon.

VESPER directly accelerates barrier crossing along the chosen CVs. Orthogonal slow motions can still limit exploration by the physical walkers. Our convergence analysis assumes overdamped dynamics and a Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition and excludes exchange, batch reuse and practical optimizers. The high-dimensional molecular results establish self-consistency and exploration without converged free-energy references. The stability controls for batch reuse (Section B.7) add per-system hyperparameters. Natural extensions are joint CV learning, adaptive level weights, and combining online sampling with existing trajectories (Section A.9).

Reproducibility statement

Proofs, protocols, scoring conventions and the algorithm are given in the appendices. VESPER is integrated into PySAGES [Zubieta Rico et al., 2024], available at https://github.com/SSAGESLabs/PySAGES. All code, run configurations and analysis scripts will be released publicly at https://github.com/JayLKap/vesper. Generative AI tools assisted with code implementation, experiment execution, figure preparation, literature review, and manuscript editing under author supervision. The authors reviewed the AI-assisted work and take full responsibility for the final content.

Appendix A Proofs

We retain the notation of the main text, with GG in energy units and α=β^/β\alpha=\hat{\beta}/\beta. When considering a single tempering level, we write PGP_{G}, νG\nu_{G}, and QGQ_{G} for PG,β^P_{G,\hat{\beta}}, νG,β^\nu_{G,\hat{\beta}}, and QG,β^Q_{G,\hat{\beta}}, respectively.

A.1 Convexity and the physical free-energy minimizer

Let pp be the physical CV density in equation 1. We work on its support 𝒮\mathcal{S}, where p>0p>0 almost everywhere, and for the chosen 0<α<10<\alpha<1 assume that

Cα=∫𝒮p​(s)α​𝑑s<∞.C_{\alpha}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}p(s)^{\alpha}\,\mathrm{d}s<\infty. (16)

We consider finite-valued measurable free energies GG for which the two normalizers

AG=∫𝒮e−β^​G​(s)​𝑑s,BG=∫𝒮p⁡(s)​e(β−β^)​G​(s)​𝑑sA_{G}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}e^{-\hat{\beta}G(s)}\,\mathrm{d}s,\qquad B_{G}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}p(s)e^{(\beta-\hat{\beta})G(s)}\,\mathrm{d}s (17)

are finite and positive.

The auxiliary density, biased microscopic density and its CV marginal are

PG​(s)=e−β^​G​(s)AG,νG​(x)=e(β−β^)​G​(s⁡(x))​ϱ​(x)BG,P_{G}(s)=\frac{e^{-\hat{\beta}G(s)}}{A_{G}},\qquad\nu_{G}(x)=\frac{e^{(\beta-\hat{\beta})G(s(x))}\varrho(x)}{B_{G}}, (18)
QG​(s)=p⁡(s)​e(β−β^)​G​(s)BG.Q_{G}(s)=\frac{p(s)e^{(\beta-\hat{\beta})G(s)}}{B_{G}}. (19)
Proposition S1 (Convexity and the free-energy minimizer).

The functional in equation 2 is convex in GG, invariant under addition of a constant, and has minimizer set {G⋆+C}\{G_{\star}+C\}. Its minimum is

ℒβ^​[G⋆]=log⁡Cαβ​α​(1−α).\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G_{\star}]=\frac{\log C_{\alpha}}{\beta\alpha(1-\alpha)}. (20)

At this minimum, PG⋆=QG⋆=pα/CαP_{G_{\star}}=Q_{G_{\star}}=p^{\alpha}/C_{\alpha}.

Proof.

Each term of equation 2 is convex by Hölder’s inequality. Adding a constant cc to GG changes the two terms by −c-c and cc, so their sum is unchanged. To identify the minimizer, differentiate in a bounded direction hh:

D​ℒβ^​[G]​(h)\displaystyle D\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G](h) =𝔼QG​h−𝔼PG​h,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{Q_{G}}h-\mathbb{E}_{P_{G}}h, (21)
D2​ℒβ^​[G]​(h,h)\displaystyle D^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G](h,h) =β^​VarPG⁡(h)+(β−β^)​VarQG⁡(h)≥0.\displaystyle=\hat{\beta}\operatorname{Var}_{P_{G}}(h)+(\beta-\hat{\beta})\operatorname{Var}_{Q_{G}}(h)\geq 0. (22)

The first variation vanishes for every such hh exactly when PG=QGP_{G}=Q_{G}. Using equation 18 and equation 19, this condition becomes

e−β^​G​(s)AG=p⁡(s)​e(β−β^)​G​(s)BG⟺G(s)=−β−1logp(s)+C.\frac{e^{-\hat{\beta}G(s)}}{A_{G}}=\frac{p(s)e^{(\beta-\hat{\beta})G(s)}}{B_{G}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G(s)=-\beta^{-1}\log p(s)+C.

To see that this candidate attains the minimum, apply Hölder’s inequality once more:

Cα=∫𝒮(e−β^​G)1−α​(p​e(β−β^)​G)α​𝑑s≤AG1−α​BGα.C_{\alpha}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}(e^{-\hat{\beta}G})^{1-\alpha}(pe^{(\beta-\hat{\beta})G})^{\alpha}\,\mathrm{d}s\leq A_{G}^{1-\alpha}B_{G}^{\alpha}.

Taking logarithms gives the lower bound in equation 20. Equality holds precisely when the two normalized factors coincide, hence precisely at G=G⋆+CG=G_{\star}+C. This candidate is admissible by equation 16, and substitution gives PG⋆=QG⋆=pα/CαP_{G_{\star}}=Q_{G_{\star}}=p^{\alpha}/C_{\alpha}. Finally, applying the chain rule to equation 21 gives the parameter gradient in equation 7, provided differentiation under the integrals is justified. ∎

A.2 KL control and endpoint limits

Proposition S2 (Loss and KL control).

Let πα=pα/Cα\pi_{\alpha}=p^{\alpha}/C_{\alpha}. Under the assumptions of proposition S1 and integrability of GG and log⁡p\log p under πα\pi_{\alpha},

ℒβ^​[G]−ℒβ^​[G⋆]=KL(πα∥PG)β^+KL(πα∥QG)β−β^.\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G]-\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G_{\star}]=\frac{\operatorname{KL}(\pi_{\alpha}\|P_{G})}{\hat{\beta}}+\frac{\operatorname{KL}(\pi_{\alpha}\|Q_{G})}{\beta-\hat{\beta}}. (23)

In particular,

KL(πα∥PG)≤β^(ℒβ^[G]−ℒβ^[G⋆]),KL(πα∥QG)≤(β−β^)(ℒβ^[G]−ℒβ^[G⋆]).\operatorname{KL}(\pi_{\alpha}\|P_{G})\leq\hat{\beta}\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G]-\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G_{\star}]\bigr),\qquad\operatorname{KL}(\pi_{\alpha}\|Q_{G})\leq(\beta-\hat{\beta})\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G]-\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G_{\star}]\bigr). (24)

At β^=β\hat{\beta}=\beta, assume ZG=∫e−β​G​𝑑s<∞Z_{G}=\int e^{-\beta G}\,\mathrm{d}s<\infty, 𝔼p​|G|<∞\mathbb{E}_{p}|G|<\infty, and 𝔼p​|log⁡p|<∞\mathbb{E}_{p}|\log p|<\infty. With qG=e−β​G/ZGq_{G}=e^{-\beta G}/Z_{G}, the extension in equation 8 satisfies

ℒβ[G]−ℒβ[G⋆]=β−1KL(p∥qG).\mathcal{L}_{\beta}[G]-\mathcal{L}_{\beta}[G_{\star}]=\beta^{-1}\operatorname{KL}(p\|q_{G}). (25)

At β^=0\hat{\beta}=0 on compact 𝒮\mathcal{S}, assume 𝔼u​|G|<∞\mathbb{E}_{u}|G|<\infty, 𝔼u​|log⁡p|<∞\mathbb{E}_{u}|\log p|<\infty, and 0<BG,0:=𝔼p​eβ​G<∞0<B_{G,0}:=\mathbb{E}_{p}e^{\beta G}<\infty. With QG,0=p​eβ​G/BG,0Q_{G,0}=pe^{\beta G}/B_{G,0}, the zero-level objective satisfies

ℒ0[G]−ℒ0[G⋆]=β−1KL(u∥QG,0).\mathcal{L}_{0}[G]-\mathcal{L}_{0}[G_{\star}]=\beta^{-1}\operatorname{KL}(u\|Q_{G,0}). (26)
Proof.

Substituting the expressions for PGP_{G} and QGQ_{G} into the two divergences gives

KL(πα∥PG)\displaystyle\operatorname{KL}(\pi_{\alpha}\|P_{G}) =𝔼πα​log⁡πα+β^​𝔼πα​G+log⁡AG,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\alpha}}\log\pi_{\alpha}+\hat{\beta}\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\alpha}}G+\log A_{G},
KL(πα∥QG)\displaystyle\operatorname{KL}(\pi_{\alpha}\|Q_{G}) =𝔼πα​log⁡πα−𝔼πα​log⁡p−(β−β^)​𝔼πα​G+log⁡BG.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\alpha}}\log\pi_{\alpha}-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\alpha}}\log p-(\beta-\hat{\beta})\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\alpha}}G+\log B_{G}.

Dividing by β^\hat{\beta} and β−β^\beta-\hat{\beta}, respectively, and adding cancels the expectations of GG. Since log⁡πα=α​log⁡p−log⁡Cα\log\pi_{\alpha}=\alpha\log p-\log C_{\alpha}, the remaining terms are ℒβ^​[G]−log⁡Cα/[β​α​(1−α)]\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G]-\log C_{\alpha}/[\beta\alpha(1-\alpha)]. This proves equation 23, and nonnegativity of either divergence gives equation 24.

At the physical endpoint, the definition in equation 8 gives directly

KL(p∥qG)=𝔼plogp+β𝔼pG+logZG=βℒβ[G]+𝔼plogp.\operatorname{KL}(p\|q_{G})=\mathbb{E}_{p}\log p+\beta\mathbb{E}_{p}G+\log Z_{G}=\beta\mathcal{L}_{\beta}[G]+\mathbb{E}_{p}\log p.

Since qG⋆=pq_{G_{\star}}=p, subtracting the same identity at G⋆G_{\star} proves equation 25.

To recover this endpoint as a limit of the interior objectives, assume in addition that ∫e−β^0​G​𝑑s<∞\int e^{-\hat{\beta}_{0}G}\,\mathrm{d}s<\infty for some 0<β^0<β0<\hat{\beta}_{0}<\beta and 𝔼p​eε0​G<∞\mathbb{E}_{p}e^{\varepsilon_{0}G}<\infty for some ε0>0\varepsilon_{0}>0. The bound e−β^​G≤e−β^0​G+e−β​Ge^{-\hat{\beta}G}\leq e^{-\hat{\beta}_{0}G}+e^{-\beta G} then gives β^−1​log⁡AG→β−1​log⁡ZG\hat{\beta}^{-1}\log A_{G}\to\beta^{-1}\log Z_{G} by dominated convergence. Writing ε=β−β^↓0\varepsilon=\beta-\hat{\beta}\downarrow 0, the difference quotient (eε​G−1)/ε(e^{\varepsilon G}-1)/\varepsilon decreases to GG and lies between the integrable functions GG and (eε0​G−1)/ε0(e^{\varepsilon_{0}G}-1)/\varepsilon_{0}. Thus 𝔼p​eε​G=1+ε​𝔼p​G+o⁡(ε)\mathbb{E}_{p}e^{\varepsilon G}=1+\varepsilon\mathbb{E}_{p}G+o(\varepsilon), so the second term of equation 2, ε−1​log⁡BG=ε−1​log⁡𝔼p​eε​G\varepsilon^{-1}\log B_{G}=\varepsilon^{-1}\log\mathbb{E}_{p}e^{\varepsilon G}, tends to 𝔼p​G\mathbb{E}_{p}G as required.

At the zero endpoint, direct expansion gives

KL(u∥QG,0)=βℒ0[G]−𝔼ulogp−log|𝒮|.\operatorname{KL}(u\|Q_{G,0})=\beta\mathcal{L}_{0}[G]-\mathbb{E}_{u}\log p-\log|\mathcal{S}|.

Since β​ℒ0​[G⋆]=𝔼u​log⁡p+log⁡|𝒮|\beta\mathcal{L}_{0}[G_{\star}]=\mathbb{E}_{u}\log p+\log|\mathcal{S}|, subtraction proves equation 26. Equality holds exactly when QG,0=uQ_{G,0}=u, or G=G⋆+CG=G_{\star}+C almost everywhere. For the renormalized limit β^↓0\hat{\beta}\downarrow 0, additionally assume ∫e−β^0​G​𝑑s<∞\int e^{-\hat{\beta}_{0}G}\,\mathrm{d}s<\infty for some 0<β^0<β0<\hat{\beta}_{0}<\beta. The same difference-quotient argument under uu gives β^−1​log⁡𝔼u​e−β^​G→−𝔼u​G\hat{\beta}^{-1}\log\mathbb{E}_{u}e^{-\hat{\beta}G}\to-\mathbb{E}_{u}G, while dominated convergence gives 𝔼p​e(β−β^)​G→BG,0\mathbb{E}_{p}e^{(\beta-\hat{\beta})G}\to B_{G,0}. These are the two terms of the renormalized limit. ∎

A.3 Dual formulation and coupled dynamics

For a probability density ρ\rho on 𝒮\mathcal{S}, define its entropy relative to the CV reference measure by Entd​s⁡(ρ)=∫𝒮ρ​log⁡ρ​𝑑s\operatorname{Ent}_{\mathrm{d}s}(\rho)=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\rho\log\rho\,\mathrm{d}s. Let ν\nu be a probability law on configuration space. Define

𝒥⁡(G,ρ,ν)=𝔼ν​[G∘s]−𝔼ρ​G−Entd​s⁡(ρ)β^−KL(ν∥ϱ)β−β^.\mathcal{J}(G,\rho,\nu)=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[G\circ s]-\mathbb{E}_{\rho}G-\frac{\operatorname{Ent}_{\mathrm{d}s}(\rho)}{\hat{\beta}}-\frac{\operatorname{KL}(\nu\|\varrho)}{\beta-\hat{\beta}}. (27)
Proposition S3 (Dual formulation and stationary sampling laws).

For 0<β^<β0<\hat{\beta}<\beta and admissible GG,

ℒβ^​[G]=supρ,ν𝒥⁡(G,ρ,ν),minG⁡ℒβ^​[G]=min⁡supρ,νG⁡𝒥⁡(G,ρ,ν).\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G]=\sup_{\rho,\nu}\mathcal{J}(G,\rho,\nu),\qquad\min_{G}\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G]=\min_{G}\sup_{\rho,\nu}\mathcal{J}(G,\rho,\nu). (28)

The maximizing laws are PGP_{G} and νG\nu_{G}, and the pushforward of νG\nu_{G} is QGQ_{G}. Suppose the potentials and CV map are smooth, the Langevin equations are well posed, and the boundaries are periodic, reflecting, or confining with sufficient decay. The fixed-model dynamics in equation 11 then preserve the configurational laws PGP_{G} and νG\nu_{G}.

Proof.

The dual identity follows by expanding the relative entropies:

𝒥⁡(G,ρ,ν)=ℒβ^​[G]−KL(ρ∥PG)β^−KL(ν∥νG)β−β^.\mathcal{J}(G,\rho,\nu)=\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G]-\frac{\operatorname{KL}(\rho\|P_{G})}{\hat{\beta}}-\frac{\operatorname{KL}(\nu\|\nu_{G})}{\beta-\hat{\beta}}. (29)

The two KL terms are nonnegative and vanish at ρ=PG\rho=P_{G} and ν=νG\nu=\nu_{G}, proving equation 28. The expansion is immediate when all terms are finite, and the Gibbs variational formula gives the same supremum otherwise.

For fixed ρ\rho and ν\nu, differentiating 𝒥\mathcal{J} with respect to θ\theta, under the integrals, gives 𝔼ν​∇θGθ∘s−𝔼ρ​∇θGθ\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}\circ s-\mathbb{E}_{\rho}\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}. At the maximizing laws this is ∇θℒβ^​[Gθ]\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G_{\theta}]. Taking the negative derivative at each level, weighting by ckc_{k}, and replacing the expectations by walker averages gives the parameter update in equation 12. Meanwhile, Wasserstein ascent in ρ\rho and ν\nu, with mobilities α/γs\alpha/\gamma_{s} and (1−α)/γx(1-\alpha)/\gamma_{x}, gives

∂tρ\displaystyle\partial_{t}\rho =γs−1​∇s⋅(α​ρ​∇sG+β−1​∇sρ),\displaystyle=\gamma_{s}^{-1}\nabla_{s}\cdot(\alpha\rho\nabla_{s}G+\beta^{-1}\nabla_{s}\rho), (30)
∂tν\displaystyle\partial_{t}\nu =γx−1​∇x⋅(ν​∇x[U−(1−α)​G∘s]+β−1​∇xν).\displaystyle=\gamma_{x}^{-1}\nabla_{x}\cdot\bigl(\nu\nabla_{x}[U-(1-\alpha)G\circ s]+\beta^{-1}\nabla_{x}\nu\bigr). (31)

Their particle realizations are the overdamped sampling equations. Adding momenta and Langevin thermostats yields the inertial realization in equation 11 with the same configurational targets.

The CV marginal of νG\nu_{G} follows from the definition of pp: for any bounded test function hh,

∫𝒳h⁡(s⁡(x))​νG​(x)​𝑑x=1BG​∫𝒮h⁡(s)​p​(s)​e(β−β^)​G​(s)​𝑑s.\int_{\mathcal{X}}h(s(x))\nu_{G}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{B_{G}}\int_{\mathcal{S}}h(s)p(s)e^{(\beta-\hat{\beta})G(s)}\,\mathrm{d}s.

Thus s#​νG=QGs_{\#}\nu_{G}=Q_{G}. To check invariance, note that the potentials α​G\alpha G and U−(1−α)​G∘sU-(1-\alpha)G\circ s at inverse temperature β\beta have Gibbs factors e−β^​Ge^{-\hat{\beta}G} and e−β​U+(β−β^)​G∘se^{-\beta U+(\beta-\hat{\beta})G\circ s}. These make the probability currents in equation 30 and equation 31 vanish. For inertial dynamics, the corresponding phase-space laws include Maxwell momentum factors: Hamiltonian transport preserves energy and phase volume, while friction and noise preserve the Maxwell factors. Under ergodicity, time averages therefore recover the required expectations.

The sampling laws also hold at β^=β\hat{\beta}=\beta, although the dual functional in equation 27 is singular there. The auxiliary potential is then GG, with invariant density PG,β∝e−β​GP_{G,\beta}\propto e^{-\beta G}, and the unbiased physical dynamics preserve ϱ\varrho. ∎

A.4 The common-minimizer ladder

Proposition S4 (Weighted excess loss and level gradients).

Assume proposition S1 at every interior level and the moment and normalizer conditions of proposition S2 at an endpoint level. For ck>0c_{k}>0 with ∑kck=1\sum_{k}c_{k}=1, the ladder functional is convex and its minimizer set is {G⋆+C}\{G_{\star}+C\}. Its parameter gradient is given by equation 10. These statements imply Proposition 1.

Proof.

For each level, propositions S1 and S2 give

Δk​[G]:=ℒβ^k​[G]−ℒβ^k​[G⋆]≥0,Δk​[G]=0⟺G=G⋆+C.\Delta_{k}[G]:=\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}_{k}}[G]-\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}_{k}}[G_{\star}]\geq 0,\qquad\Delta_{k}[G]=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ G=G_{\star}+C.

This includes both endpoints by equation 25 and equation 26. The excess of the combined objective is ∑kck​Δk​[G]\sum_{k}c_{k}\Delta_{k}[G]. Since every ckc_{k} is positive, this sum vanishes exactly when every component vanishes, proving the common-minimizer claim. Each component is convex and invariant under constant shifts, so the weighted sum has both properties as well. At either endpoint, these properties follow directly from equation 8: the log-partition term is convex, the expectation is linear, and their shifts cancel. If the model family contains G⋆+CG_{\star}+C, it attains the same minimum.

Finally, differentiating the finite sum gives

∇θℒVESPER​[Gθ]=∑kck​∇θℒβ^k​[Gθ].\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VESPER}}[G_{\theta}]=\sum_{k}c_{k}\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}_{k}}[G_{\theta}].

Substitution of equation 7 proves equation 10. At the physical endpoint, differentiating equation 8 gives 𝔼p​∇θGθ−𝔼PGθ,β​∇θGθ\mathbb{E}_{p}\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}-\mathbb{E}_{P_{G_{\theta},\beta}}\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}, assuming differentiation under the integral is justified. This has the same form, since νG,K=ϱ\nu_{G,K}=\varrho and s#​ϱ=ps_{\#}\varrho=p. At the zero endpoint the gradient is 𝔼QGθ,0​∇θGθ−𝔼u​∇θGθ\mathbb{E}_{Q_{G_{\theta},0}}\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}-\mathbb{E}_{u}\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}, again assuming justified differentiation, with PGθ,0=uP_{G_{\theta},0}=u and s#​νGθ,0=QGθ,0s_{\#}\nu_{G_{\theta},0}=Q_{G_{\theta},0}. Thus each level contributes expectations under its own sampling laws, with coefficient ckc_{k}. ∎

A.5 Replica-exchange acceptance

Proposition S5 (Exchange preserves the level product laws).

Fix GG for which all level distributions are normalizable, and consider replicas of the same physical system at inverse temperature β\beta, with auxiliary inverse temperatures β^k\hat{\beta}_{k}. A symmetric proposal to swap two physical configurations, accepted with AxA_{x} in equation 15, is reversible with respect to ∏kνG,k\prod_{k}\nu_{G,k}. The analogous auxiliary swap with acceptance AsA_{s} is reversible with respect to ∏kPG,k\prod_{k}P_{G,k}.

Proof.

For an auxiliary swap between levels ii and jj, the ratio of the swapped and original product densities is

PG,i​(sj)​PG,j​(si)PG,i​(si)​PG,j​(sj)=exp⁡[(β^i−β^j)​(G⁡(si)−G⁡(sj))].\frac{P_{G,i}(s^{j})P_{G,j}(s^{i})}{P_{G,i}(s^{i})P_{G,j}(s^{j})}=\exp\!\left[(\hat{\beta}_{i}-\hat{\beta}_{j})(G(s^{i})-G(s^{j}))\right].

For a physical swap, write Gi=G⁡(s⁡(xi))G_{i}=G(s(x^{i})) and Gj=G⁡(s⁡(xj))G_{j}=G(s(x^{j})). The common physical factors ϱ⁡(xi)​ϱ​(xj)\varrho(x^{i})\varrho(x^{j}) and the normalizers cancel, leaving

log⁡νG,i​(xj)​νG,j​(xi)νG,i​(xi)​νG,j​(xj)\displaystyle\log\frac{\nu_{G,i}(x^{j})\nu_{G,j}(x^{i})}{\nu_{G,i}(x^{i})\nu_{G,j}(x^{j})} =(β−β^i)​Gj+(β−β^j)​Gi\displaystyle=(\beta-\hat{\beta}_{i})G_{j}+(\beta-\hat{\beta}_{j})G_{i}
−(β−β^i)​Gi−(β−β^j)​Gj\displaystyle\quad-(\beta-\hat{\beta}_{i})G_{i}-(\beta-\hat{\beta}_{j})G_{j}
=(β^i−β^j)​(Gi−Gj).\displaystyle=(\hat{\beta}_{i}-\hat{\beta}_{j})(G_{i}-G_{j}).

Thus the two log ratios are

ℓs=(β^i−β^j)​[G⁡(si)−G⁡(sj)],ℓx=(β^i−β^j)​[Gi−Gj].\ell_{s}=(\hat{\beta}_{i}-\hat{\beta}_{j})[G(s^{i})-G(s^{j})],\qquad\ell_{x}=(\hat{\beta}_{i}-\hat{\beta}_{j})[G_{i}-G_{j}]. (32)

In either case, let TT denote the swap and Π\Pi the product density. Since T2​z=zT^{2}z=z, the Metropolis acceptance A⁡(z)=min⁡{1,Π⁡(T​z)/Π⁡(z)}A(z)=\min\{1,\Pi(Tz)/\Pi(z)\} satisfies Π⁡(z)​A​(z)=min⁡{Π⁡(z),Π⁡(T​z)}=Π⁡(T​z)​A​(T​z)\Pi(z)A(z)=\min\{\Pi(z),\Pi(Tz)\}=\Pi(Tz)A(Tz). Together with the symmetric proposal, this proves detailed balance. With equal masses and a common thermostat, the Maxwell factors also cancel if momenta are exchanged. Leaving momenta in place preserves the same independent Maxwell law. Composing pair-exchange kernels therefore preserves Π\Pi. A joint symmetric swap of both populations instead uses the sum ℓx+ℓs\ell_{x}+\ell_{s} as its log acceptance ratio. ∎

A.6 Convergence of the coupled population dynamics

We now consider the overdamped population dynamics with continuous parameter descent and no replica exchange. The aim is to control the objective error together with the lag of the sampling distributions behind their changing targets.

First suppose that all levels satisfy 0<αk<10<\alpha_{k}<1, with ck>0c_{k}>0 and ∑kck=1\sum_{k}c_{k}=1. We treat the physical endpoint below. It is convenient to use dimensionless quantities,

gθ=β​Gθ,F⁡(θ)=β​ℒVESPER​[Gθ],fθ​(s)=∇θgθ​(s),g_{\theta}=\beta G_{\theta},\qquad F(\theta)=\beta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VESPER}}[G_{\theta}],\qquad f_{\theta}(s)=\nabla_{\theta}g_{\theta}(s),

so the instantaneous targets are

Pkθ​(s)=e−αk​gθ​(s)Ak​(θ),νkθ​(x)=ϱ⁡(x)​e(1−αk)​gθ​(s⁡(x))Bk​(θ).P_{k}^{\theta}(s)=\frac{e^{-\alpha_{k}g_{\theta}(s)}}{A_{k}(\theta)},\qquad\nu_{k}^{\theta}(x)=\frac{\varrho(x)e^{(1-\alpha_{k})g_{\theta}(s(x))}}{B_{k}(\theta)}. (33)

Let ρk,t\rho_{k,t} and νk,t\nu_{k,t} denote the evolving auxiliary and physical laws. Suppressing the time subscript inside expectations, their equations are

These weights will cancel the tempering factors when we differentiate the relative entropies.

Let F∗=minθ⁡F⁡(θ)F_{*}=\min_{\theta}F(\theta) be finite and attained. We make the following assumptions on an open neighborhood 𝒪\mathcal{O} of the initial sublevel {θ:F⁡(θ)≤F⁡(θ0)+H0}\{\theta:F(\theta)\leq F(\theta_{0})+H_{0}\}:

    I(ζ∥Pkθ)≥2λs,kKL(ζ∥Pkθ),I(ζ∥νkθ)≥2λx,kKL(ζ∥νkθ),I(\zeta\|P_{k}^{\theta})\geq 2\lambda_{s,k}\operatorname{KL}(\zeta\|P_{k}^{\theta}),\qquad I(\zeta\|\nu_{k}^{\theta})\geq 2\lambda_{x,k}\operatorname{KL}(\zeta\|\nu_{k}^{\theta}),

    where I(ζ∥π)=∫∥∇log(ζ/π)∥2dζI(\zeta\|\pi)=\int\|\nabla\log(\zeta/\pi)\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\zeta. With constants positive and uniform on 𝒪\mathcal{O}, set a=mink⁡{ds,k​λs,k,dx,k​λx,k}>0a=\min_{k}\{d_{s,k}\lambda_{s,k},d_{x,k}\lambda_{x,k}\}>0.

In (C3), the physical inequality is required for the full microscopic law. Uniform constants follow, for example, from the Holley–Stroock perturbation lemma when the model gives a uniformly bounded tilt of a reference law satisfying a log-Sobolev inequality [Holley & Stroock, 1987].

Under (C1)–(C4), for 0<η<a/B20<\eta<a/B^{2}, the evolution in equation 34 obeys

A.7 General reference measures

The same variational argument applies to a general reference measure. Let rr be sigma-finite and let the probability measure pp have density f=d​p/d​r>0f=\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}r>0 rr-almost everywhere. For r=d​sr=\mathrm{d}s, this ff is the physical CV density p⁡(s)p(s). Writing g=β​Gg=\beta G, define

ℓα​[g]=1α​log​∫e−α​g​𝑑r+11−α​log​∫e(1−α)​g​𝑑p.\ell_{\alpha}[g]=\frac{1}{\alpha}\log\int e^{-\alpha g}\,\mathrm{d}r+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\log\int e^{(1-\alpha)g}\,\mathrm{d}p. (42)

For the physical Lebesgue reference, ℓα​[β​G]=β​ℒβ^​[G]\ell_{\alpha}[\beta G]=\beta\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G]. When Zg=∫e−g​𝑑r<∞Z_{g}=\int e^{-g}\,\mathrm{d}r<\infty, the normalized residual model is

qg​(d​y)=Zg−1​e−g⁡(y)​r​(d​y).q_{g}(\mathrm{d}y)=Z_{g}^{-1}e^{-g(y)}r(\mathrm{d}y). (43)
Proposition S8 (Reference-measure minimizer).

For 0<α<10<\alpha<1 with M⁡(α)=∫fα​𝑑r<∞M(\alpha)=\int f^{\alpha}\,\mathrm{d}r<\infty, the functional in equation 42, restricted to gg for which both integrals are finite, is minimized exactly at g⋆=−log⁡f+Cg_{\star}=-\log f+C. At the minimum, the two tilted laws coincide with fα​d​r/M⁡(α)f^{\alpha}\mathrm{d}r/M(\alpha).

Proof.

As in the proof of proposition S1, Hölder’s inequality gives

M⁡(α)=∫(e−α​g)1−α​(f​e(1−α)​g)α​𝑑r≤(∫e−α​g​𝑑r)1−α​(∫e(1−α)​g​𝑑p)α.M(\alpha)=\int(e^{-\alpha g})^{1-\alpha}(fe^{(1-\alpha)g})^{\alpha}\,\mathrm{d}r\leq\left(\int e^{-\alpha g}\,\mathrm{d}r\right)^{1-\alpha}\left(\int e^{(1-\alpha)g}\,\mathrm{d}p\right)^{\alpha}.

Equality requires the two factors to be proportional, which is equivalent to g=−log⁡f+Cg=-\log f+C. At this choice, both normalized densities relative to rr equal fα/M⁡(α)f^{\alpha}/M(\alpha). ∎

A.8 Positive-weight effective sample size

Proposition S9 (Population normalized ESS).

At the population optimum, the fixed-data weights are proportional to fα−1f^{\alpha-1}. If M⁡(2​α−1)<∞M(2\alpha-1)<\infty, their population normalized effective sample size is

(𝔼p​w)2𝔼p​w2=M​(α)2M⁡(2​α−1).\frac{(\mathbb{E}_{p}w)^{2}}{\mathbb{E}_{p}w^{2}}=\frac{M(\alpha)^{2}}{M(2\alpha-1)}. (44)

For independent yj∼py_{j}\sim p with wj=w⁡(yj)w_{j}=w(y_{j}), the empirical quantity (∑jwj)2/[n​∑jwj2](\sum_{j}w_{j})^{2}/[n\sum_{j}w_{j}^{2}] converges to this value almost surely. At α=1/2\alpha=1/2, the denominator is M⁡(0)=r⁡(supp⁡p)M(0)=r(\operatorname{supp}p).

Proof.

The scale of the weights cancels in the ratio, so take w=fα−1w=f^{\alpha-1}. Since d​p=f​d​r\mathrm{d}p=f\mathrm{d}r, we have 𝔼p​w=∫fα​𝑑r=M⁡(α)\mathbb{E}_{p}w=\int f^{\alpha}\,\mathrm{d}r=M(\alpha) and 𝔼p​w2=∫f2​α−1​𝑑r=M⁡(2​α−1)\mathbb{E}_{p}w^{2}=\int f^{2\alpha-1}\,\mathrm{d}r=M(2\alpha-1), proving equation 44. The assumed second moment allows the strong law of large numbers to be applied to both empirical moments, giving the almost-sure limit. ∎

A.9 Learning from existing data

When equilibrium configurations xj∗∼ϱx_{j}^{*}\sim\varrho are already available, their CV values yj=s⁡(xj∗)y_{j}=s(x_{j}^{*}) can replace the physical walkers. The physical expectation in equation 7 is then estimated using normalized importance weights

w¯j​(θ)=e(β−β^)​Gθ​(yj)∑ℓe(β−β^)​Gθ​(yℓ).\bar{w}_{j}(\theta)=\frac{e^{(\beta-\hat{\beta})G_{\theta}(y_{j})}}{\sum_{\ell}e^{(\beta-\hat{\beta})G_{\theta}(y_{\ell})}}. (45)

This leads to the following weighted-data consistency result.

Proposition S10 (Weighted-data gradient).

Fix θ\theta and let xj∗x_{j}^{*} be independent samples from ϱ\varrho, with yj=s⁡(xj∗)y_{j}=s(x_{j}^{*}). Suppose BGθ<∞B_{G_{\theta}}<\infty and 𝔼p​[e(β−β^)​Gθ​‖∇θGθ‖]<∞\mathbb{E}_{p}[e^{(\beta-\hat{\beta})G_{\theta}}\|\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}\|]<\infty. Then the weights in equation 45 satisfy

∑j=1nw¯j​(θ)​∇θGθ​(yj)⟶𝔼νGθ​∇θGθ∘salmost surely as ​n→∞.\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bar{w}_{j}(\theta)\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}(y_{j})\longrightarrow\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{G_{\theta}}}\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}\circ s\quad\text{almost surely as }n\to\infty. (46)

Moreover, the corresponding weighted population objective has minimizer G⋆+CG_{\star}+C.

Proof.

Using the CV marginal in equation 19, the required expectation can be written as

𝔼νGθ​∇θGθ∘s=𝔼p​[e(β−β^)​Gθ​∇θGθ]𝔼p​[e(β−β^)​Gθ].\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{G_{\theta}}}\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}\circ s=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{p}[e^{(\beta-\hat{\beta})G_{\theta}}\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}]}{\mathbb{E}_{p}[e^{(\beta-\hat{\beta})G_{\theta}}]}.

The assumed moments allow the strong law of large numbers to be applied to both sample averages. Their ratio converges almost surely because the limiting denominator is positive, proving equation 46.

Together with the auxiliary expectation, this yields the gradient in equation 7 of the original population objective, whose minimizer is G⋆+CG_{\star}+C by proposition S1. The exponential weighting is essential: using unweighted samples from pp would instead give the functional stationarity condition PG=pP_{G}=p, equivalently G=G⋆/α+CG=G_{\star}/\alpha+C. ∎

The auxiliary walkers still sample PGθP_{G_{\theta}}, so the resulting update is a weighted-data version of the same learning rule. With g=β​Gg=\beta G and γ=α−1\gamma=\alpha-1, the objective coincides with the PS-CD/γ\gamma-cross-entropy objective continued to negative γ\gamma [Yu et al., 2021, Fujisawa & Eguchi, 2008], with the Rényi variational representation described in Appendix D [Birrell et al., 2021].

The same ratio argument also yields within-population sample-reuse weights. If a batch was generated at G0G_{0}, then the current-to-generating density ratios are proportional to

w(s)=e−β^​(G−G0),w(x)=e(β−β^)​(G−G0)∘s.w^{(s)}=e^{-\hat{\beta}(G-G_{0})},\qquad w^{(x)}=e^{(\beta-\hat{\beta})(G-G_{0})\circ s}. (47)

Normalization within each pool removes the unknown partition functions:

𝔼PG0​[w(s)​f]=AGAG0​𝔼PG​f,𝔼νG0​[w(x)​f∘s]=BGBG0​𝔼νG​f∘s.\mathbb{E}_{P_{G_{0}}}[w^{(s)}f]=\frac{A_{G}}{A_{G_{0}}}\,\mathbb{E}_{P_{G}}f,\qquad\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{G_{0}}}[w^{(x)}f\circ s]=\frac{B_{G}}{B_{G_{0}}}\,\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{G}}f\circ s.

Hence, if GG and G0G_{0} are admissible, ff is integrable under the current law, and the batch satisfies a law of large numbers under its generating law, the corresponding self-normalized estimators are consistent. Their weight concentration is monitored by the ESS criterion described in Appendix E.

The single-level update also admits a scalar-objective interpretation in self-consistent well-tempered VES. For Vθ=−(1−α)​GθV_{\theta}=-(1-\alpha)G_{\theta} and the instantaneous target tθ=PGθt_{\theta}=P_{G_{\theta}}, differentiating the VES functional while holding tt fixed gives

∇θΩ​[Vθ;t]|t=tθ=(1−α)​∇θℒβ^​[Gθ].\left.\nabla_{\theta}\Omega[V_{\theta};t]\right|_{t=t_{\theta}}=(1-\alpha)\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G_{\theta}]. (48)

The target convention and the recursive neural VES update are detailed in Section D.1 [Valsson & Parrinello, 2014, Valsson & Parrinello, 2015, Bonati et al., 2019].

Appendix B Physical systems: models and protocols

This appendix gives the model, force field, collective-variable and network settings behind Section 3, together with the trust region, readout and gauge conventions used for every number reported there.

Unless stated otherwise, reported estimates are means ±\pm sample standard deviations across independent runs. Errors are computed for each run before averaging. Free-energy maps formed by averaging model predictions before marginalization are identified explicitly. Molecular times are per physical replica, and aggregate MD is summed over replicas.

B.1 Alanine dipeptide

System and CVs.

Explicit-solvent alanine dipeptide, AMBER99SB [Hornak et al., 2006] with TIP3P water [Jorgensen et al., 1983] and particle-mesh Ewald electrostatics, 298.15 K, 2 fs timestep, bonds to hydrogen constrained. The CVs are the backbone dihedrals ϕ,ψ\phi,\psi, both periodic.

Model and training.

GθG_{\theta} is a SIREN [Sitzmann et al., 2020] with one hidden layer of width 3232, ω0=16\omega_{0}=16 and a periodic input embedding. Each replica carries 10410^{4} auxiliary walkers with γs=10\gamma_{s}=10 and γx=100\gamma_{x}=100. Training uses AdamW [Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019] at learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, up to 8080 inner iterations per epoch, and epochs of 10001000 MD steps, 5050 per checkpoint (100100 ps). The single replica uses α=0.01\alpha=0.01. Both four-level ladders use α=(0.1,0.05,0.02,0.01)\alpha=(0.1,0.05,0.02,0.01) with equal loss weights. L-RE attempts exchange of physical configurations between adjacent levels every epoch. L-NRE uses the same ladder without exchange. The single replica starts from the same configurations as the OPES runs.

Reference and analysis.

The reference surface is the free energy from 100 ns of adaptive-biasing-force sampling by Zubieta Rico et al. [2025], on a 100×100100\times 100 periodic grid. Figure 3 reports mean-aligned RMSE over this full grid. OPES and TAMD are scored only on cells where their native free-energy estimators are finite. VESPER predictions use parameter averages over the trailing eight available checkpoints, or all available checkpoints at earlier times. RMSE curves average the individual-run errors. The displayed surfaces average the mean-aligned predictions and shift the resulting minimum to zero. Physical points overlaid on the maps are drawn from the last nanosecond and auxiliary points from the final saved populations, balanced across runs and ladder levels.

B.2 Alanine tetrapeptide

System and CVs.

Gas-phase Ace-(Ala)3-NMe, AMBER99SB [Hornak et al., 2006] without cutoff, 298.15 K, 2 fs timestep, bonds to hydrogen constrained. The three-CV model biases (ϕ1,ϕ2,ϕ3)(\phi_{1},\phi_{2},\phi_{3}) and the six-CV model adds ψ1\psi_{1}, ψ2\psi_{2} and ψ3\psi_{3}.

Model and training.

GθG_{\theta} is a SIREN with hidden widths (14,4)(14,4), ω0=16\omega_{0}=16 and a periodic input embedding, so the two models differ only in the input layer (163163 and 247247 parameters). Each replica carries 2×1042\times 10^{4} auxiliary walkers with γs=γx=100\gamma_{s}=\gamma_{x}=100. Training uses AdamW at 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, up to 8080 inner iterations, and epochs of 10001000 steps, 100100 per checkpoint (200200 ps). The single replica uses α=0.01\alpha=0.01, and the ladder arms are those of ADP. Both models train at a constant step size throughout. Each model is read as the parameter-SWA10 average over checkpoints from 8.2–10.0 ns.

Readout and analysis.

Temporal correlations compare trailing ten-checkpoint parameter averages ending at 5 and 10 ns, using windows of 3.2–5.0 and 8.2–10.0 ns, respectively. Pearson correlations are calculated on 262,144 evaluation points pooled from four scrambled Sobol sets spanning the full six-dimensional CV domain. Reported values are the mean and sample standard deviation across three independent runs.

Figure 4 shows physical Boltzmann marginals at 298.15 K. The full physical free-energy predictions from the three independent runs of the four-level exchange ladder are averaged before Boltzmann integration and marginalization. The retained (ϕ1,ϕ2)(\phi_{1},\phi_{2}), (ϕ1,ϕ3)(\phi_{1},\phi_{3}) and (ϕ2,ϕ3)(\phi_{2},\phi_{3}) planes are complete 64×6464\times 64 grids. Six-CV maps integrate omitted ψ\psi coordinates on 32-point axes and the remaining omitted ϕ\phi on its 64-point grid, while three-CV maps integrate the omitted ϕ\phi on a 256-point grid. Display surfaces are shifted to zero minimum and use a common 0–120 kJ mol-1 scale with 10 kJ mol-1 contours. The three-to-six-CV squared-Pearson correlations over all plane cells are 0.9510.951, 0.8950.895 and 0.8900.890.

B.3 Chignolin

System and CVs.

CLN025 [Honda et al., 2008] in explicit solvent, ff14SB [Maier et al., 2015] with TIP3P [Jorgensen et al., 1983], 340 K, 2 fs timestep, with its seventeen backbone dihedrals as CVs. Structural deviation is measured by Cα\alpha root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) after Kabsch superposition [Kabsch, 1976].

Model and training.

GθG_{\theta} is a SIREN with hidden widths (48,24)(48,24), ω0=1\omega_{0}=1 and a periodic input embedding (2,8812{,}881 parameters). Twelve replicas span a geometric ladder from α=1\alpha=1 to α=1/18\alpha=1/18, every level exchanging physical configurations with its neighbors every epoch. Each carries 10510^{5} auxiliary walkers. Training uses AdamW at learning rate 10−410^{-4} with a gradient clip of 10​kB​T10\,k_{B}T, up to 100100 inner iterations and epochs of 50005000 steps, 2020 per checkpoint (200200 ps), at constant step throughout. Four independent runs extend to 26.226.2 ns per replica, and the readout is the final checkpoint.

Readout and analysis.

Frames are saved every 55 ps, 5,2405{,}240 per level and run. Full-run occupancy fractions and exchange acceptance pool the four runs over 26.226.2 ns. Every reported unfolding and refolding event falls within the first 2525 ns. Folded and unfolded are defined as Cα\alpha RMSD below 0.200.20 nm and above 0.400.40 nm. An unfolding or refolding event requires the new state to persist for 2020 ps and is counted along each configuration’s identity. This dwell criterion is not applied to the framewise occupancy estimates.

The time-resolved occupancies in Fig. 6A,B use non-overlapping 0.20.2 ns bins, each containing 4040 saved frames per run. At each saved time, configurations are assigned to their current tempering levels before RMSD classification. For panel B, the within-bin folded fractions at each level are averaged equally across the four runs. For panel A, each run’s per-level fractions are summed to give the time-averaged numbers of levels in each state. The lines show their mean and the bands their minimum-to-maximum range across runs. Both panels display bins in the first 2525 ns. The reported 99.3%99.3\% unbiased-level occupancy uses the full 26.226.2 ns trajectory.

The learned surfaces are estimated from 25,00025{,}000 auxiliary walkers of the unbiased level drawn at random from each run at the readout (100,000100{,}000 in all), and the MD frames shown in Fig. 6C come from the last nanosecond. For the radius-of-gyration and RMSD map, each walker’s dihedrals are placed on a backbone with the bond lengths, bond angles, peptide ω\omega and Pro4 ϕ\phi of the native structure, and F=−kB​T​ln⁡pF=-k_{B}T\ln p (kB​T=2.83k_{B}T=2.83 kJ mol-1), with pp an adaptive Gaussian kernel density estimate. The dihedral maps are product von Mises kernel density estimates, compared after mean alignment with the same estimate on the unbiased level’s MD frames where the MD free energy is below 1010 kJ mol-1. Over (ϕ2,ψ2)(\phi_{2},\psi_{2}), (ψ3,ψ4)(\psi_{3},\psi_{4}) and (ϕ5,ψ5)(\phi_{5},\psi_{5}), the learned minimum lies 0.420.42, 0.070.07 and 0.190.19 rad from the MD minimum, at points where the MD free energy is 1.31.3, 0.20.2 and 0.50.5 kJ mol-1 above its minimum, with RMS differences of 1.91.9, 2.22.2 and 2.02.0 kJ mol-1. Accepted exchanges permute configurations between levels, so every configuration keeps its identity (Section A.5).

B.4 Catalytic methane dehydrogenation

System and CVs.

Methane on stepped Ni(511) at 700700 K uses an Allegro machine-learned interatomic potential [Musaelian et al., 2023], deployed through the NequIP toolchain [Batzner et al., 2022] and driven by OpenMM [Eastman et al., 2017]. The CVs are the two coordination numbers of Jin et al. [2025] and the periodic fractional coordinate S1S_{1} of the carbon atom along the first surface lattice vector. The system has 8585 atoms, 2525 held fixed, in a triclinic cell. A soft restraint keeps the system in the CV ranges: S1∈[0,1]S_{1}\in[0,1], CNi∈[0.05,3.02]\mathrm{CNi}\in[0.05,3.02], and CH∈[2.95,3.98]\mathrm{CH}\in[2.95,3.98].

Model and training.

GθG_{\theta} is a SIREN with hidden widths (14,4)(14,4) and ω0=16\omega_{0}=16. One replica at α=0.05\alpha=0.05 carries 6.5×1046.5\times 10^{4} auxiliary walkers, using AdamW at learning rate 10−410^{-4}, with up to 100100 inner iterations and epochs of 50005000 steps, 2020 per checkpoint, at a 0.250.25 fs timestep, so one checkpoint is 2525 ps. Training uses a gradient clip of 50​kB​T50\,k_{B}T, γs=100\gamma_{s}=100, γx=10\gamma_{x}=10, Langevin friction 9.829.82 ps-1 and a constant step. The reweighted inner step uses the full trust region of Section B.7. Three independent runs extend to checkpoint 300. Each checkpoint-300 physical free-energy prediction uses deployed parameter EMA decay 0.90.9.

B.5 Catalysis free-energy projections

With S1S_{1} the periodic fractional coordinate and y,zy,z the C–Ni and C–H coordination numbers, the two-dimensional free energies shown in Fig. 5 are Boltzmann marginals of the equal-weight mean of the three gauge-aligned checkpoint-300 EMA predictions,

FR(qR)=−kBTlog∫DO​(qR)exp[−Gmean(qR,qO)/(kBT)]dqO,F_{R}(q_{R})=-k_{B}T\log\int_{D_{O}(q_{R})}\exp[-G_{\rm mean}(q_{R},q_{O})/(k_{B}T)]\,\mathrm{d}q_{O},

at T=700T=700 K, with ordinary measure in the original CV coordinates and integration box D=S1​[0,1]×y⁡[0.02,3]×z⁡[2.90,3.94]D=S_{1}[0,1]\times y[0.02,3]\times z[2.90,3.94], while the visible route uses S1​[0.02,0.98]×y⁡[0.10,2.95]×z⁡[2.97,3.94]S_{1}[0.02,0.98]\times y[0.10,2.95]\times z[2.97,3.94]. Each map is shifted to its own minimum for display. The route is initialized by a string-method calculation on the differentiable mean surface and refined by constrained gradient flow, resolving contacts with the route bounds. This yields a locally resolved route within the stated box, but global path optimality is not established. The physisorbed representative is constrained at the lower C–Ni route bound, and the fitted saddle is at S1≈0.65S_{1}\approx 0.65, near the step-edge atoms at S1≈0.70S_{1}\approx 0.70. The route’s G⁡(3)−G⁡(1)=1.12G(3)-G(1)=1.12 eV is a bounded surface difference. Its 0.250.25 eV uncertainty is the sample standard deviation of the individual model differences evaluated at the same reactant and saddle points on the mean-surface route.

B.6 Ladder configuration by system

Table 1 lists the levels of every molecular system. Each level is one physical trajectory. The auxiliary walkers enter only the training loss. The single-level runs of ADP and ATP use α=0.01\alpha=0.01, and ADP also has a single-level run at α=1\alpha=1.

B.7 Reweighted inner steps and the step-size controller

Within an epoch the walker samples generated under Gθ0G_{\theta_{0}} are frozen while several parameter steps are taken and reweighted by self-normalized importance sampling at every step (Section 2.4). A trust region bounds the log-weights: a soft threshold δ=5\delta=5 on their 9595th percentile, a hard threshold δhard=8\delta_{\mathrm{hard}}=8 on their maximum, and a floor of 0.20.2 on the effective sample size of the pool. Exceeding the hard threshold or falling below the floor ends the epoch and forces fresh trajectory data. Exceeding the soft threshold multiplies the parameter step by 1/q21/q^{2} with q=∥log⁡w∥95/δq=\lVert\log w\rVert_{95}/\delta. It is used on ADP, ATP and catalysis. Chignolin trains on fresh samples only.

On ADP, the inner-iteration budget and learning rate are governed by a sample-based controller rather than a predefined schedule. The controller latches a decay phase when cumulative relative parameter change across checkpoints exceeds a budget of 160%160\%, then multiplies the learning rate by 0.950.95 and the inner-iteration count by 0.70.7 per checkpoint, flooring the count at 55. Once the count reaches its floor and the learning rate is below 5%5\% of its initial value, a final phase continues the decay to a floor of 0.3%0.3\% and deploys an exponential moving average (EMA) of parameters with decay 0.990.99 per epoch. ATP uses constant-step training.

B.8 Readout, optimizer settings and RMSE gauge

Models use system-specific parameter readouts. ATP predictions use a uniform average of the last ten checkpoints, and ADP uses the last eight available checkpoints. At the reported horizon these ADP parameters have already undergone EMA smoothing. These are the Polyak–Ruppert or stochastic-weight-averaging (SWA) readouts [Polyak & Juditsky, 1992, Ruppert, 1988, Izmailov et al., 2018]. Catalysis uses the deployed EMA readout with decay 0.90.9 at checkpoint 300, and chignolin reports its final checkpoint (26.226.2 ns per replica). AdamW [Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019] uses decoupled weight decay w=0.01w=0.01 in every run, and the peptide runs apply the cautious mask of Liang et al. [2026], which zeroes coordinates whose Adam step is not descent-aligned with the current gradient and rescales the rest.

RMSE is reported after removing the additive constant. Mean alignment, used for ADP, removes the mean difference between the learned and reference surfaces on the scored region. Flat-surface baselines, where reported, use the same region and gauge. ATP dimensional-consistency comparisons use complete retained planes, squared-Pearson correlations and mean-aligned RMSEs after physical Boltzmann marginalization.

B.9 Baseline settings

The ADP and ATP comparisons in Sections 3.2 and 3.3 use the Hamiltonians and CVs specified above and a 2 fs timestep. The no-exchange control retains the ladder’s architecture and population sizes. In ADP and ATP, auxiliary moves swap whole populations and were accepted in at most 0.5%0.5\% of epochs over 10 ns. Most accepted exchanges transport physical configurations. ADP VESPER single-replica, OPES and TAMD runs share initial configurations. Means and sample standard deviations use the trajectories that reach the reported horizon.

OPES uses bias factor 100 and barrier parameter 4040 kJ mol-1 [Invernizzi & Parrinello, 2020]. Metadynamics deposits 1.21.2 kJ mol-1 hills every 500 steps [Laio & Parrinello, 2002], and TAMD uses UFEDMM [Bajpai et al., 2023]. Readouts are the OPES kernel density, the negative metadynamics hill sum, and the TAMD auxiliary-variable histogram at its own temperature. CFF [Sevgen et al., 2020] and its SIREN variant (S-CFF) [Zubieta Rico et al., 2025] use their saved native free-energy functions. ADP errors use the full-grid convention for methods with finite estimates and the native finite-estimator-cell convention for OPES and TAMD.

Neural VES.

We test this method using the released code [Bonati et al., 2019]. The bias factor is 100, with 50 grid bins per periodic CV and ReLU widths 4848–2424–1212 for ADP. Adam starts at 10−310^{-3}. Parameter and target updates occur every 500 MD steps with the released system-specific learning-rate controllers. Errors use the native free-energy exports.

B.10 Compute

Table 2 lists the simulated time per replica at the readout and the resulting aggregate MD per run. Several runs continued beyond the readout, and the table counts MD up to it. The ADP baselines are OPES, metadynamics, TAMD, neural VES, CFF and S-CFF. VESPER, CFF and S-CFF ran on NVIDIA H100, H200, L40S and RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, and the other baselines on CPUs, so wall-clock times are not comparable across methods. For scale, one chignolin run takes about 100 h on one H100 GPU, which runs all twelve replicas, and one methane run takes about 140–180 GPU-hours, mostly on L40S GPUs.

B.11 Reported molecular results

Table 3 collects the values quoted in Sections 3.2, 3.3, 3.4 and 3.5, with the readout behind each.
