C.2 Four-well dimensional scaling

Landscape.

The reference landscape has four symmetric Gaussian components whose centers lie in a fixed two-dimensional plane involving all dd coordinates. Up to an additive constant, its thermal-unit form is

G⋆​(s)kB​T=−log∑a,b∈{−1,1}exp[−‖s−δ⁡(a​v1+b​v2)‖22​σw2],δ=1.6,σw=0.3.\frac{G_{\star}(s)}{k_{B}T}=-\log\sum_{a,b\in\{-1,1\}}\exp\!\left[-\frac{\|s-\delta(av_{1}+bv_{2})\|^{2}}{2\sigma_{w}^{2}}\right],\qquad\delta=1.6,\quad\sigma_{w}=0.3.

Here v1=(1,…,1)/dv_{1}=(1,\ldots,1)/\sqrt{d}, and v2v_{2} is obtained by orthogonalizing the alternating-sign vector against v1v_{1} and normalizing it. The remaining directions are harmonic, with dimensionless curvature 1/σw21/\sigma_{w}^{2}. The adjacent-well barriers are approximately 13.5​kB​T13.5\,k_{B}T. The CV map is the identity, and the dynamics use reflecting boundaries on [−3,3]d[-3,3]^{d}. The two-dimensional core is identical at every dd. The reference contains 40,00040{,}000 i.i.d. draws from the analytic teacher Boltzmann distribution, and errors use all dd coordinates.

Protocol.

d∈{2,5,10,25,50,100}d\in\{2,5,10,25,50,100\}. The same three-hidden-layer network of width 1024 is used at every dd. A separate perfect-information regression of the exact free energy into this network (i.i.d. Boltzmann samples, exact energies, 160,000160{,}000 Adam updates of batch 1,0001{,}000) establishes that it can represent the four-well plane at d=100d=100 (widths 128, 256 and 512 do not learn the d=100d=100 plane, while width 1024 reaches a plane error of 0.030.03–0.13​kB​T0.13\,k_{B}T against 1.291.29 for a flat surface at every dd). The primary arms use 1,0001{,}000 physical and 1,0001{,}000 auxiliary walkers in total, both started in the deepest well, 160,000160{,}000 overdamped steps at Δ​t=0.005\Delta t=0.005 (reduced time 800800), Adam at 3×10−53\times 10^{-5}, a bias-corrected parameter EMA with time constant 2,0002{,}000 steps for the convergence readout and a trailing-half parameter average for the endpoint. Arms: single levels at α=1\alpha=1, 0.50.5, 0.250.25, 0.10.1, 0.050.05, and four-level ladders (α=0.5\alpha=0.5, 0.250.25, 0.10.1, 0.050.05; 250250 walkers per level and population) with and without symmetric exchange of physical and auxiliary walkers. As a control on population rather than temperature, the same ladders were also run with 1,0001{,}000 walkers per level and population. Three independent runs were specified per arm. The unbiased d=2d=2 arm uses its two completed runs, and all other arms use three.

Readouts.

NRMSE=RMSE/σ\mathrm{NRMSE}=\mathrm{RMSE}/\sigma, where the RMSE is the teacher-Boltzmann-weighted full-coordinate error after removing the additive constant and σ\sigma is the corresponding standard deviation of the reference free energy. The endpoint NRMSE uses the trailing-half SWA readout, while threshold time uses the bias-corrected EMA readout. The reduced threshold time is when the EMA NRMSE first stays below 0.250.25 to the end of the run. DKL(ρ∥ρθ)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\rho\,\|\,\rho_{\theta}) uses the same teacher-Boltzmann reference samples. Endpoint summaries are means ±\pm sample SD (Tables 5 and 6). For threshold-time summaries, a run that never reaches the sustained threshold is capped at the budget of 800800.

Observations.

The same exchange ladder is within a factor of 1.621.62 of the best tested single level on mean NRMSE across all dimensions. Its mean NRMSE ranges from 0.190.19 to 0.420.42, with lower mean error than the best single level at d=50d=50 and 100100. At d=100d=100, the primary exchange and no-exchange ladders reach 0.32±0.210.32\pm 0.21 and 0.40±0.190.40\pm 0.19, respectively, while the best single level reaches 0.42±0.050.42\pm 0.05. The larger-population controls reach 0.39±0.200.39\pm 0.20 with exchange and 0.33±0.110.33\pm 0.11 without (Table 6). These descriptive comparisons support one fixed ladder across the tested dimensions. They do not establish uniform superiority or an exchange advantage at every dimension.

Appendix D Connections to VES, PS-CD, and Rényi objectives

The following identities connect the VESPER objective to well-tempered VES, pseudo-spherical contrastive divergence, and a Rényi variational principle.

D.1 Well-tempered VES and an explicit shared-energy objective

Let pp be the physical CV density and tt the VES target. The fixed-target functional of Valsson & Parrinello [2014] is

Ω⁡[V;t]=β−1​log⁡𝔼p​e−β​V+∫t⁡(s)​V​(s)​𝑑s.\Omega[V;t]=\beta^{-1}\log\mathbb{E}_{p}e^{-\beta V}+\int t(s)V(s)\,\mathrm{d}s.

Differentiating with tt held fixed gives

∇θΩ​[Vθ;t]=−𝔼biased​∇θVθ+𝔼t​∇θVθ.\nabla_{\theta}\Omega[V_{\theta};t]=-\mathbb{E}_{\rm biased}\nabla_{\theta}V_{\theta}+\mathbb{E}_{t}\nabla_{\theta}V_{\theta}.

Set Vθ=−(1−α)​GθV_{\theta}=-(1-\alpha)G_{\theta} and tθ=PGθt_{\theta}=P_{G_{\theta}}, with 0<α<10<\alpha<1. The biased physical law is then νGθ\nu_{G_{\theta}}, and substitution yields

∇θΩ​[Vθ;t]|t=tθ=(1−α)​{𝔼νGθ​∇θGθ∘s−𝔼PGθ​∇θGθ}=(1−α)​∇θℒβ^​[Gθ].\left.\nabla_{\theta}\Omega[V_{\theta};t]\right|_{t=t_{\theta}}=(1-\alpha)\left\{\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{G_{\theta}}}\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}\circ s-\mathbb{E}_{P_{G_{\theta}}}\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}\right\}=(1-\alpha)\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}}[G_{\theta}].

This proves equation 48 for every admissible model for which differentiation under the integrals is valid. The factor 1−α1-\alpha can be absorbed into the step size for ordinary gradient descent with the same parameterization and sample estimate.

VESPER thus gives the instantaneous self-consistent update an explicit scalar objective, convex in the free energy. This point requires holding the VES target fixed during differentiation. Taking the total derivative of Ω⁡[Vθ;tθ]\Omega[V_{\theta};t_{\theta}] also differentiates the target and adds

∫Vθ​(s)​∇θtθ​(s)​𝑑s=α​β​(1−α)​Covtθ⁡(Gθ,∇θGθ),\int V_{\theta}(s)\nabla_{\theta}t_{\theta}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s=\alpha\beta(1-\alpha)\operatorname{Cov}_{t_{\theta}}(G_{\theta},\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}),

where we used ∇θtθ=−α​β​tθ​(∇θGθ−𝔼tθ​∇θGθ)\nabla_{\theta}t_{\theta}=-\alpha\beta t_{\theta}(\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}-\mathbb{E}_{t_{\theta}}\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}). In contrast, differentiating ℒβ^\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}} directly gives the desired two-population update, with its minimum and KL control established in propositions S1 and S2.

The distinction also appears in how the target evolves. Well-tempered VES sets t∝pαt\propto p^{\alpha} [Valsson & Parrinello, 2015]. In neural VES, the free-energy relation F^=−V−β−1​log⁡t\widehat{F}=-V-\beta^{-1}\log t and the previous target tn−1∝e−α​β​F^n−1t_{n-1}\propto e^{-\alpha\beta\widehat{F}_{n-1}} give the recursive update [Bonati et al., 2019]

F^n=−Vn+α​F^n−1+Cn,tn∝e−α​β​F^n.\widehat{F}_{n}=-V_{n}+\alpha\widehat{F}_{n-1}+C_{n},\qquad t_{n}\propto e^{-\alpha\beta\widehat{F}_{n}}. (49)

At a fixed point, (1−α)​F^=−V+C(1-\alpha)\widehat{F}=-V+C, so V=−(1−α)​GV=-(1-\alpha)G gives F^=G+const\widehat{F}=G+\mathrm{const}. During learning, VESPER instead defines the target directly from the current GθG_{\theta} and represents it with persistent auxiliary walkers. One model therefore determines both the molecular bias and the auxiliary potential, without a separate recursion for the free-energy estimate. The walker laws track these changing targets through the coupled dynamics analyzed in Section A.6.

This formulation extends directly to the combined objective: every ℒβ^k\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\beta}_{k}} has the same physical minimizer, so all levels train one GθG_{\theta} through their native gradients (Proposition 1). In VES notation, the interior-level update is reproduced by weighting the corresponding fixed-target gradients by ck/(1−αk)c_{k}/(1-\alpha_{k}). The rescaled gradient has the finite physical-endpoint limit

limα↑111−α​∇θΩ​[−(1−α)​Gθ;t]|t=PGθ=𝔼p​∇θGθ−𝔼PGθ,β​∇θGθ,\lim_{\alpha\uparrow 1}\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\left.\nabla_{\theta}\Omega[-(1-\alpha)G_{\theta};t]\right|_{t=P_{G_{\theta}}}=\mathbb{E}_{p}\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta}-\mathbb{E}_{P_{G_{\theta},\beta}}\nabla_{\theta}G_{\theta},

whenever the two expectations converge. VESPER includes this endpoint through equation 8.

D.2 PS-CD and direct sampling of the two tilted populations

With g=β​Gg=\beta G, the dimensionless objective ℓα\ell_{\alpha} is given by equation 42. Let qg=e−g/Zgq_{g}=e^{-g}/Z_{g} be the model density relative to a reference measure rr, with Zg<∞Z_{g}<\infty. Substituting log⁡qg=−g−log⁡Zg\log q_{g}=-g-\log Z_{g} and γ=α−1\gamma=\alpha-1 gives

ℓα​[g]=11+γ​log​∫qg1+γ​𝑑r−1γ​log​∫qgγ​𝑑p=ℒγPS​[g].\ell_{\alpha}[g]=\frac{1}{1+\gamma}\log\int q_{g}^{1+\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}r-\frac{1}{\gamma}\log\int q_{g}^{\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}p=\mathcal{L}^{\rm PS}_{\gamma}[g]. (50)

The first term contributes −log⁡Zg-\log Z_{g} and the second +log⁡Zg+\log Z_{g}, so the normalizer cancels. This is the PS-CD objective [Yu et al., 2021], including its negative-γ\gamma extension, whenever both integrals are finite. For VESPER, 0<α<10<\alpha<1 gives γ=α−1∈(−1,0)\gamma=\alpha-1\in(-1,0). The physical free-energy minimizer follows from proposition S1.

For the Lebesgue reference, write qθ=qGθ=e−β​Gθ/ZGθq_{\theta}=q_{G_{\theta}}=e^{-\beta G_{\theta}}/Z_{G_{\theta}}. The two populations in the gradient are exactly the laws used in the main text:

PGθ​(s)\displaystyle P_{G_{\theta}}(s) =qθ​(s)α∫qθ​(u)α​𝑑u,\displaystyle=\frac{q_{\theta}(s)^{\alpha}}{\int q_{\theta}(u)^{\alpha}\,\mathrm{d}u}, (51)
QGθ​(s)\displaystyle Q_{G_{\theta}}(s) =p⁡(s)​qθ​(s)α−1∫p⁡(u)​qθ​(u)α−1​𝑑u.\displaystyle=\frac{p(s)q_{\theta}(s)^{\alpha-1}}{\int p(u)q_{\theta}(u)^{\alpha-1}\,\mathrm{d}u}.

Differentiating the two log integrals gives ∇θℓα​[gθ]=𝔼QGθ​∇θgθ−𝔼PGθ​∇θgθ\nabla_{\theta}\ell_{\alpha}[g_{\theta}]=\mathbb{E}_{Q_{G_{\theta}}}\nabla_{\theta}g_{\theta}-\mathbb{E}_{P_{G_{\theta}}}\nabla_{\theta}g_{\theta}, recovering equation 7 after division by β\beta. At the physical endpoint, PGθ=qθP_{G_{\theta}}=q_{\theta} and QGθ=pQ_{G_{\theta}}=p, recovering the maximum-likelihood gradient.

The computational difference is how these expectations are obtained. PS-CD uses a fixed dataset for the positive term and reweights samples from qθq_{\theta} to estimate the tempered model expectation [Yu et al., 2021]. VESPER directly evolves auxiliary walkers in α​Gθ\alpha G_{\theta}, removing that temperature-change importance weighting from the fresh-sample gradient. In molecular applications, it also generates QGθQ_{G_{\theta}} online through the biased microscopic law νGθ\nu_{G_{\theta}}. This makes the same variational principle usable when equilibrium configurations are not available in advance: sampling supplies new configurations while their gradients update the free-energy model (Section A.3).

D.3 Rényi variational identity and its sampling realization

For a probability reference rr and 0<α<10<\alpha<1, set h=−gh=-g in equation 42. Then

−ℓα​[g]=1α−1​log​∫e(α−1)​h​𝑑p−1α​log​∫eα​h​𝑑r,-\ell_{\alpha}[g]=\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\log\int e^{(\alpha-1)h}\,\mathrm{d}p-\frac{1}{\alpha}\log\int e^{\alpha h}\,\mathrm{d}r,

which is the variational expression of Birrell et al. [2021, Theorem 3.1]. With f=d​p/d​r>0f=\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}r>0 rr-almost everywhere and M⁡(α)=∫fα​𝑑rM(\alpha)=\int f^{\alpha}\,\mathrm{d}r, proposition S8 gives g⋆=−log⁡f+Cg_{\star}=-\log f+C. Substituting this minimizer into the two integrals yields

infgℓα[g]=log⁡M⁡(α)α⁡(1−α)=−1αDα(p∥r),Dα(p∥r)=log⁡M⁡(α)α−1.\inf_{g}\ell_{\alpha}[g]=\frac{\log M(\alpha)}{\alpha(1-\alpha)}=-\frac{1}{\alpha}D_{\alpha}(p\|r),\qquad D_{\alpha}(p\|r)=\frac{\log M(\alpha)}{\alpha-1}.

The factor 1/α1/\alpha accounts for the divergence convention in that reference. If ff vanishes on a set of positive rr-measure, the infimum need not be attained by a finite free energy.

The value of this identity for VESPER is that its optimizer is also the quantity needed to drive sampling. For r=d​sr=\mathrm{d}s, g⋆=β​G⋆g_{\star}=\beta G_{\star} up to a constant. VESPER uses GθG_{\theta} to bias microscopic dynamics and to evolve the auxiliary walkers, obtaining both gradient expectations without evaluating the unknown CV density pp or first collecting equilibrium data (Section A.3). The KL decomposition in proposition S2 connects the objective excess to the discrepancy of PGP_{G} and QGQ_{G} from their common tempered target, and Proposition 1 lets several orders train the same physical free energy.

For a reference of finite mass RR, normalization to r/Rr/R subtracts (log⁡R)/α(\log R)/\alpha from ℓα\ell_{\alpha} and leaves its gradients unchanged. On infinite-volume CV domains we instead use the exponential integrals directly, with the integrability conditions of Sections A.1 and A.7. This preserves the same free-energy minimizer without introducing an artificial uniform probability reference.

Appendix E Algorithm and implementation details

VESPER is implemented in PySAGES [Zubieta Rico et al., 2024]. We alternate molecular and auxiliary sampling with parameter updates, retaining the auxiliary population between epochs. Neural models provide both parameter derivatives for learning and spatial derivatives for biasing. When several parameter updates reuse one batch, within-population importance weights account for the change from its generating model. The pseudocode and weight formulas are given below. Model architectures, integration parameters, optimizer settings, exchange intervals, and readouts are specified for each experiment in Appendix B.

Algorithm 1 describes physical sampling with an energy-unit model GθG_{\theta} and level ratios αk=β^k/β\alpha_{k}=\hat{\beta}_{k}/\beta. Each epoch generates physical and auxiliary samples, optionally exchanges configurations (predominantly physical configurations in the reported ADP and ATP runs, Appendix B), and updates the shared model.

Sample reuse.

The weights of equation 47 supply the two density ratios for a batch generated at Gθ0G_{\theta_{0}}. Reweighted estimators also appear in Carbone et al. [2023] and Invernizzi & Parrinello [2020]. The molecular implementation can monitor the 95th percentile and maximum of |log⁡w||\log w|, with soft and hard thresholds 55 and 88, and the normalized ESS (∑w)2/[n​∑w2](\sum w)^{2}/[n\sum w^{2}], with floor 0.20.2. Activation, step reduction, and refresh rules are specified per system in Section B.7.

Existing-data updates.

For equilibrium observations xj∗∼ϱx_{j}^{*}\sim\varrho, replace physical sampling and its reuse weights by equation 45.

Checkpoint and averaged readouts.

A trailing weight-space average produces a network with parameters

θ¯=1|W|​∑k∈Wθk.\bar{\theta}=\frac{1}{|W|}\sum_{k\in W}\theta_{k}. (52)

The checkpoint set WW, stride, and window are specified per experiment [Polyak & Juditsky, 1992, Izmailov et al., 2018]. Fixed-checkpoint and last-iterate readouts use their corresponding θk\theta_{k}.
